doc.title: Mike Davis interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2024

title: How rock artists get horn parts: Stones, Bobby Keys, Paul Simon
summary: Davis explains the Stones worked with Bobby Keys without written charts, Simon mixes arrangers and band input, and simple lines suit rock.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: So these fellas like this, they have arrangers who write out the horn parts for the most part. Is that correct?

Yeah. For the most part, yeah. I mean the Stones for instance did not, and we would use whatever, at that time Bobby Keys, who was kind of their most important and main sax guy, he recorded all those original solos on “Brown Sugar” and “Rip This Joint” and all the tenor solos were played by Bobby. And Bobby was, you know the section leader for sure and so we would kind of — would interface with Bobby in how we were going to — what horn lines we were playing. So occasionally they would ask us to come up with some horn arrangement if you want to say it that way. But and there was no music because they don’t read or write music. I mean they write music but they don’t read music so there as no — and in fact in the M.D., who was Chuck Leavell, who is a keyboard player, he couldn’t read music either. So there was no need for charts per se but I mean their catalogue is so vast that we had to keep kind of little cheat sheets just to remember the stuff. And it’s remarkable that they can remember all the tunes. And they tap into their catalogue. They change it up from tour to tour, they change the set quite a bit. So I mean they’re obligated like any big star to play the big hits, but yeah, so for them we would come up with arrangements but they were mostly just done without writing anything down. Other bands for sure. Paul Simon I think is in-between. I don’t think he — he does hire arrangers but then at other times he’ll just work with his band and talk
about what he wants. People will kind of add their input in kind of an organic creative process.
Yeah that’s like going to graduate school when you get in those situations. Like you can learn what you had at Eastman but you’ve got to add your own ear and intuition.

A hundred percent. And you know there’s a personal dynamic too because you want to know how far you can add input. Because some people don’t really want much more than what they’re saying and you have to try to interpret that and translate it into working for the horns. And then in the case of, like my experience with the Stones with Bobby, you know we wanted to make sure he was comfortable with everything so we had to be — you know we just had to be aware, you know, of who could get bent out of shape if you start imposing too much information or you know it’s too — for lack of a better word — too slick or something, if it’s something like the Stones or Bob Dylan or something like that. It’s not going to work to have complicated horn lines and complex voiced out things. So I mean I wasn’t always aware of it. I became more aware of it as time went by but it makes — it really makes me appreciate like the Sinatra thing that we talked about earlier, just walking in and just an absolute gold — a pile of gold there and all you’ve got to do is sit down and just play your little part of it and it’s going to be fun and great.
